newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-Supersonic or breeze-speed, Cape Town offers all.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Supersonic or breeze-speed, Cape Town offers all.

text.p: Float silently over vineyards laced with tendrils of dawn mist or hurtle vertically to 60,000 feet (18,000 metres) in a thundering twin-jet Lightning T5 and plunge back to earth at twice the speed of sound.
These are the extremes of a range of flying experiences that make South Africa's foremost tourist city the Cape of Flight for increasing numbers of visitors.

Between the breeze-speed of the hot-air balloon and the jet experience beyond the sound barrier are helicopter rides, a seaplane take-off from among the cranes of Cape Town harbour and a flight in a 1932 Junkers JU-52 with wind-down windows.

"Cape Town happens to be a bit of a Mecca for aviation enthusiasts," said Peter Claxton, owner and pilot of Flamingo Flights, which flies tourists from the city's Waterfront entertainment centre in a 1954 De Havilland Beaver seaplane.
"Everybody has this boyish fancy of going up in the air and you can see a lot more than you can on the ground," he said.

Claxton's reconditioned Beaver, workhorse of the Canadian waterways, operates from a jetty in the Victoria and Alfred docks where tall ships berthed at the height of the Dutch East India Company's trade with the Far East three centuries ago.
LANDING AMONG DOLPHINS AND WHALES

Port control slots his take-offs and landings in among the comings and goings of pilot boats, tugs and tankers. The flotilla of tour boats has come to recognise the distinctive roar of the plane's Pratt and Whitney R985 rotary engine and keeps out of the way.

"When the water is absolutely flat, we can land virtually anywhere. If we see...whales, dolphins or seals, we get the direction they're swimming in, we land on the water ahead of them and they swim up to us and around us," said Claxton.

Cape Town is best known for its landmark Table Mountain, its white, sandy beaches and the vineyards 30 minutes inland from the castle established in 1652 by Hollander Jan van Riebeeck, the first European settler.

Increasingly, however, the city offers special experiences for adventure seekers bored by the thought of another day of sunbathing or yet another glass of chilled Cape wine beneath a centuries-old oak tree.
ULTIMATE THRILL

"We offer the ultimate thrill for people who have tried everything else," said Mike Beachy Head, whose Classic Jets South Africa claims to be the only civilian operator in the world licensed to fly paying customers in supersonic military jets.
"It started off as fun and it still is fun, but I have been quite amazed at the fascination of the general public for this thing," he said.
Though he will fly a visitor in one of his immaculately restored British jets for upwards of 6,000 rand ($1,280) for 30 minutes, he prefers his passengers to take his $35,000 10-day package.
The trip, including first class travel from anywhere in the world, five-star hotels and a personal tour itinerary, is built around five flights totalling about four and a half hours in the air.

The first in a two-seater Hawker Hunter T8 is a gentle tour of the Cape Peninsula, from Cape Point to Table Mountain. But the tempo builds, including aerobatics, a low-level dash down the coast in a British Aerospace Buccaneer SB2F and a high speed trip through rugged mountain valleys.
The climax comes in the final flight when Beachy Head goes offshore and from 35,000 feet (10,700 metres), points the shark-like nose of his black Lightning at the sky and fires the afterburners.
BACK TO THE EARTH AT MACH TWO, THEN A BEER

"At 60,000 feet you can see the stars and for a moment you'll be as high as just about anyone else has ever been. Then we come down at Mach Two (twice the speed of sound). And then we go home for a beer," he said.

At the opposite end of the spectrum is South Africa's slowest registered airline, Udo Mettendorf's Wineland Ballooning, offering dawn flights over the vineyards west of the picturesque wine-making town of Paarl.
Getting aboard for the one-hour, 880 rand flight is rare because the weather allows for only 20 to 30 flights a year.

But for Ann Sturrock, for whom the flight was a 50th birthday present, it was well worth getting up at 4 a.m. on the morning after Christmas to be ready for the 6:15 a.m. takeoff from a field alongside a gabled Cape Dutch farmhouse.

"It was magnificent, unbelievable...what a wonderful way to see the Cape," she said after the balloon's woven basket had bumped gently to the ground in a mown wheatfield from which the mist was still clearing.
The most common tourist flight is a helicopter ride over Table Mountain from a landing pad in the busy Waterfront.

CivAir helicopter tour manager James Blomerus said many passengers were escaping the crush of four-hour queues at tourist attractions like the cable-car which takes visitors to the top of Table Mountain.
NO BETTER WAY TO SEE CAPE TOWN
"I don't think there is a better way to see Cape Town than from the air," he said.
"It's a growth industry for us...the main thing we are going to have to worry about is the noise pollution problem as more and more helicopters start to operate over the mountain."
Business had grown fourfold since President Nelson Mandela's election in 1994 put an end to South Africa's international isolation under apartheid.
One French tour operator has a regular booking for up to 40 people every Monday, but most of the business is from groups of two or four people, often American, British or German.
"It was thrilling and absolutely beautiful...You really get to see everything from up there," said Heather Huisamen after a 20-minute trip along the seafront and back around the mountain.

And then there's "Tante Ju", the lumbering German-built Junkers JU 52 used by state-owned South African Airways for its first scheduled flights to Europe in 1934 and now restored and back again as flag-carrier of SAA's fleet of historic airliners.
"You can have an action-packed flying holiday in Cape Town without even getting your feet wet," said Civair's Blomerus.
